hints: Notice that each statement is really describing a different halogen in disguise, so start by translating words like highest boiling point and most volatile into Cl2, Br2 or I2.
Remember that iodine is the biggest molecule so it has the highest boiling point, while chlorine is the smallest so it is the most volatile and forms the strongest bond to hydrogen.
Now compare the trends, boiling point increases down the group but H-X bond strength, thermal stability and oxidising power all decrease down the group, to see which statements mix them up.
walkthrough:
**Translate the descriptions into named halogens**

Think like a detective. Boiling point depends on instantaneous dipole (id-id) forces, which get stronger with more electrons.

$$\text{boiling point: } \mathrm{I_2 > Br_2 > Cl_2}$$
So highest boiling point and strongest id-id both mean iodine, while most volatile (lowest boiling point) means chlorine.

**Check statement 1 about H-X bond strength**

Bond strength to hydrogen depends on atomic size and orbital overlap. Smaller halogen atoms overlap better with hydrogen.

$$\text{H-X bond strength: } \mathrm{H-Cl > H-Br > H-I}$$
Statement 1 says iodine forms the strongest bond to hydrogen, but it actually forms the weakest. So statement 1 is false.

**Check statement 2 about thermal stability**

Thermal stability of $\mathrm{HX}$ follows the same order as bond strength. The stronger the bond, the more heat needed to break it.

$$\text{thermal stability: } \mathrm{HCl > HBr > HI}$$
Statement 2 says iodine (strongest id-id) forms the most stable $\mathrm{HX}$, but $\mathrm{HI}$ is the least stable and decomposes most easily on heating. So statement 2 is false.

**Check statement 3 about oxidising hydrogen**

Oxidising power decreases down Group 17 because smaller atoms gain electrons more readily.

$$\text{oxidising power: } \mathrm{Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2}$$
The most volatile element is chlorine, and chlorine is also the strongest oxidiser, so it oxidises hydrogen (to $\mathrm{HCl}$) most rapidly and vigorously. So statement 3 is true, giving 3 only.

options.A: Incorrect. Both 1 and 2 link the iodine trend (high boiling point, strong id-id) to the chlorine trend (strong H-X bond, stable HX). In fact the trends are opposite down the group, so both statements are false.
options.B: Incorrect. Statement 1 is false. The highest boiling point halogen is iodine, but the strongest H-X bond is H-Cl, not H-I, because the small Cl atom gives better overlap with H.
options.C: Incorrect. Statement 2 is false even though statement 3 is true. The halogen with strongest id-id forces is iodine, but the most thermally stable hydrogen halide is HCl, not HI.
options.D: Correct. Only statement 3 is true. Chlorine is the most volatile (lowest boiling point) and also the strongest oxidising agent of the three, so it most rapidly oxidises hydrogen to form HCl.
